title: Hannah's Prayer and Samuel's Birth
summary: Elkanah, a man from the hill country of Ephraim, goes up each year to worship at Shiloh with his two wives, Hannah, who has no children, and Peninnah, who has several and taunts her. In bitter grief Hannah prays silently at the shrine and vows that if the LORD gives her a son she will give him back to the LORD for life. Eli the priest first mistakes her for a drunk, then blesses her; she bears Samuel, and when he is weaned she brings him to Shiloh to serve the LORD.
story: The book of Judges ended in chaos: no king, a shrine at Shiloh, tribes at war with one another, and everyone doing what was right in their own eyes. First Samuel begins in that same world, and it begins small. There is no army or national crisis, only a family at a festival and a woman who can't have children. The pattern is familiar from Genesis, where Sarah, Rebekah, and Rachel all struggled with barrenness before bearing sons through whom God carried his promise forward, and from Judges 13, where Samson was born to a childless mother. When the Bible opens a new chapter in Israel's history with a barren woman, the reader should expect God to do something that human strength can't. The boy Hannah dedicates will become the prophet who anoints Israel's first two kings.
historical:
The events belong to the end of the period of the judges, probably in the eleventh century BC, a generation or so before Saul became king (usually dated around 1050 BC). Israel was a federation of tribes without a central government, and the Philistines, settled on the coastal plain to the west, were growing in power. Shiloh, about twenty miles north of Jerusalem in the territory of Ephraim, was the site of the main sanctuary, where the ark of the covenant had been kept since the days of Joshua (Joshua 18:1). The chapter calls it the house and temple of the LORD, with a doorpost where Eli sits, so by this time the sanctuary seems to have included a more permanent structure as well as the tent.

Elkanah is introduced as an Ephraimite from Ramathaim-zophim, the town later simply called Ramah, whose exact location is debated. First Chronicles 6 lists Elkanah and Samuel in the genealogy of the Levites. Some explain the difference by saying Elkanah was a Levite living in Ephraim's territory; others think Chronicles later incorporated Samuel into the Levitical line because of his priestly role. The text of 1 Samuel itself does not raise the question.
cultural:
In the ancient Near East a woman's security and standing depended heavily on bearing children, especially sons, who would carry on the family's name and care for their parents in old age. Barrenness was painful, socially shameful, and often read as a sign of divine disfavor. Taking a second wife when the first was childless was an accepted practice, and the Bible's stories of such households (Abraham with Sarah and Hagar, Jacob with Leah and Rachel) consistently show the rivalry and grief it produced. Peninnah is literally called Hannah's rival, a word used for a co-wife.

The yearly sacrifice was a family feast. Part of a peace offering was burned for the LORD, part went to the priest, and the rest was eaten by the worshipers, which is why Elkanah hands out portions. Hannah's vow that no razor would touch her son's head recalls the Nazirite vow of Numbers 6, a special dedication to God usually taken for a limited time, here made for a whole life. Children were typically weaned much later than today, often around age two or three, so Samuel was still very young when he was brought to Shiloh. Praying aloud was normal in the ancient world; Hannah's silent prayer, with moving lips and no sound, was unusual enough that Eli misread it.
literary: The chapter is a carefully shaped narrative that moves from barrenness to birth to dedication. It opens like the story of Samson's parents in Judges 13 (there was a man from a town, his name was...), signaling a birth story of a deliverer. The dialogue does much of the work: Elkanah's well-meant but uncomprehending question, “Am I not better to you than ten sons?” (verse 8); Eli's harsh misjudgment; and Hannah's dignified reply that she has “poured out my soul before the LORD” (verse 15). The key word is the Hebrew verb sha'al, to ask, which runs through the chapter: Hannah asks, Eli prays God will grant what she asked, she names the boy because she asked for him, and at the end she gives him back, using a form of the same verb that means lent or dedicated. That form is also the name Saul, and many readers think the wordplay quietly anticipates the king the people will ask for later in the book.

outline.t: Yearly worship at Shiloh and Hannah's grief
The LORD remembers Hannah: Samuel is born
Samuel weaned and given to the LORD at Shiloh

doctrines.note: Hannah's prayer is honest, bitter, and persistent. She brings her grief to God rather than hiding it, and the text calls it pouring out her soul. The chapter shows that God hears prayer made in anguish, and that prayer is not a matter of correct words or public performance.

The narrator says twice that the LORD had closed Hannah's womb and then that the LORD remembered her. Life and its opening are in God's hands. That does not make Hannah's suffering simple, but it means her story is not governed by chance or by her rival.
A family's private sorrow becomes the start of Israel's national renewal. God answers one woman's prayer in a way that serves his purposes for the whole people, a pattern the book will repeat.

words.note: Sha'al, to ask. The verb appears five times in the chapter and ties its scenes together: Hannah's petition, Eli's blessing, the naming of Samuel, and the dedication, where a form meaning lent or given on request is used. The passive participle, sha'ul, is the same as the name Saul, which is why many scholars see a hint here of the king Israel will soon ask for.

Nadar, to vow. A vow was a solemn promise to God, often conditional (if you do this, I will do that). Israelite law took vows seriously and allowed a husband to confirm or cancel his wife's vow (Numbers 30). Elkanah lets Hannah's stand, and she keeps it at great personal cost.

Tseva'ot, Hosts, in the title LORD of Hosts. This chapter is the first place in the Bible where the title appears. The hosts are armies, either heavenly armies of angels and stars or Israel's forces, and the title presents the LORD as the commander of all powers. It is fitting that a desperate woman at the edges of society addresses God by this title.

Palal, to pray. The common verb for prayer, especially intercession. The chapter distinguishes Hannah's prayer from ritual: she prays in her heart, with lips moving and no sound, and the priest cannot read it. It anticipates the song of prayer that opens chapter 2.

christ: Luke's Gospel deliberately echoes this chapter. Elizabeth, like Hannah, is childless and conceives by God's gift, and Mary's song after the annunciation (Luke 1:46-55) closely follows the themes of Hannah's song in the next chapter. Luke's description of the boy Jesus growing in favor with God and people (Luke 2:52) mirrors the wording about Samuel in 1 Samuel 2:26, and Jesus, like Samuel, is presented at the sanctuary by his parents (Luke 2:22). The link is one of pattern and allusion rather than prediction: Samuel is not a type of Christ in every detail, but his birth belongs to a biblical pattern in which God brings deliverance through a child given against human odds, a pattern that reaches its fullest expression in the birth of Jesus.

hard.q: How could a mother give away her young child, and was it right to make such a vow?
hard.a: To modern readers, leaving a small child at a sanctuary can sound like abandonment. The text presents it differently. Samuel is placed in the care of the high priest at the nation's central shrine, a position of honor, and Hannah continues to visit him yearly and make him clothes (2:19). Parents in the ancient world often apprenticed children young, and dedicating a child to a sanctuary was a known, if rare, practice. Still, the story does not pretend it was easy; Hannah's vow costs her the son she longed for, and the narrator honors her for keeping it. Some readers also note the irony that Samuel is left in the house of Eli, whose own sons are corrupt, and see God's protection of the boy as part of the point. The chapter does not command parents to do what Hannah did. It describes a costly act of faith in which a woman gives back to God the gift she most wanted.

questions: Elkanah loves Hannah but doesn't understand her grief, and Eli misreads her prayer entirely. How can you listen to people in pain without minimizing or misjudging what they are carrying?
Hannah brought her bitterness to God honestly rather than hiding it. What would it look like for you to pour out your soul before the LORD?
Hannah gave back the very gift she had prayed for. What good gift in your life do you hold most tightly, and what would it mean to hold it as belonging to God?
